# Evolution and revolution: Personality research for the coming world of robots, artificial intelligence, and autonomous systems

## A R T I C L E I N F O

Keywords: Personality Artificial intelligence Human-robot interaction Trust Autonomous systems

## A B S T R A C T

In forty years, human existence will be radically transformed by advances in information technology, including Artificial Intelligence, robots capable of social agency, and other autonomous physical and virtual systems. Future personality research must assess, understand, and apply individual differences in adaptation to these novel challenges. This review article discusses directions for future personality research. Cross-cultural research provides a model, in that both universal traits and those specific to future society are needed. Evolution of major “etic” trait models of today will maintain their relevance. There is also scope for defining a range of new “emic” dimensions for constructs such as trust in autonomy, mental models for robots, anthropomorphism of technology, and preferences for communication with machines. A more revolutionary perspective is that availability of big data on the individual will revive idiographic perspectives. Both nomothetic and idiographic accounts of personality may support applications such as design of intelligent systems and products that adapt to the individual.

## 1. Introduction

Forty years from now, the information revolution will have completely transformed the physical, virtual, and social landscapes that human beings inhabit. Intelligent autonomous systems, powered by advances in computing hardware and software, as well as more facile and intimate human-system integration, will be an especially potent driver of change. Powerful systems will include intelligent robots operating in settings such as the military, advanced healthcare, autonomous transportation, and augmented and ubiquitous decision-making software agents. We know that this will be so because the foundations for all these innovations are evident in our own times. Technological advancements will produce a series of interlocked challenges that people may well not be adequately prepared to meet.

The central aim of this article is to anticipate developments in personality psychology that may inform individual differences research in future societies shaped by symbiosis between humans and intelligent artificial systems, including machines and virtual agents. We draw on contemporary developments in personality assessment and the human factors of human-machine interaction to project some promising avenues for research, including evolution of contemporary trait theory, as well as more revolutionary change in constructs and approaches.

## 1.1. Challenges of future technology

## 1.1.1. Cognitive challenges

Advances in artificial intelligence (AI) are increasingly hard to comprehend, even for subject matter experts (SMEs). The ordinary individual is not (and perhaps cannot be) equipped to understand the intricacies and nuances of machine learning, data-mining, and distributed computing; especially when such areas of technical expertise are themselves moving so quickly. Indeed, the vastly different time scales over which human and machine information-processing operate may preclude even a general understanding; a phenomenon known as “incommensurate temporality” (Hancock, 2019a). Conventional cognitive abilities and related processing competencies will remain important. For example, existing research shows that operator usage of automation correlates with spatial ability (Chen & Barnes, 2012) and with working memory (Rovira, Pak & McLaughlin, 2017) . However, general intelligence, based on application of rule-based principles, may be of limited use in understanding how advanced AI is actually functioning. Instead, the key individual difference (ID) factors may be those that support a tolerance of such ignorance, assigning appropriate trust to such AI within a specific context, and informed dynamic decision making based on integration of inputs from such AI sources with other information to combine with human knowledge and acquisition. Future ID research can build on existing studies of domain knowledge (Goff & Ackerman, 1992) and dynamic decision making (Nicholson & O'Hare, 2014) to identify factors relevant to adaptive utilization of AI. The uncertainty intrinsic to human comprehension of AI also highlights the relevance of decision-making factors. For example, bias in perceptions of personal competence may be related to under-utilization of automation (Schaffer, O'Donovan, Michaelis, Raglin & Höllerer, 2019). IDs in cognitive ability and related constructs are beyond our present scope, but they will likely interact with personality in shaping the person's interactions with technology.

## 1.1.2. Self-regulative challenges

Humans prefer to see themselves as the pinnacle of evolution. However, this perception may have to change as artificial systems become increasingly adept at decision-making and navigating the complex physical and social landscapes of real life. Robots are already designed to express social agency and attitudes, supported by anthropomorphic design (Złotowski, Proudfoot, Yogeeswaran & Bartneck, 2015). Furthermore, machines and humans will become increasingly symbiotic (Hancock, 2007, 2019a, 2019b). The needs of young adults for constant smartphone access may be only the beginning of an ever-increasing symbiosis or co-dependence. The machine may require ever-richer information from the human to function effectively. The implications of co-dependence for the human self and identity promise to be profound. For example, people require social creativity to maintain a healthy identity when faced by advanced machine capabilities that pose an “outgroup” threat to human distinctiveness (Cha et al., 2020).

## 1.1.3. Cultural challenges

Cultures inevitably change with technological advances, but the cultural shifts associated with the information revolution are especially impactful. For example, group affiliations may evolve to include non-humans: Fraune, Sabanovic and Smith (2017) found that, in a competitive teaming situation, participants preferred ingroup robots to outgroup humans. For all the benefits of information technology, there are also dark aspects associated with vulnerability to manipulation by those who control AI, loss of privacy, and damage to the information infrastructure caused by fake news and other forms of deception. Given the current pace of change, we anticipate large and persistent generational differences; many of today's young or digital natives are assured of being tomorrow's digital dinosaurs.

These challenges, in their turn, raise questions about the ID factors that will mediate between success and failure in the coming world of 2060. Which personal traits will shape whether a person can team effectively with advancing AI? How will the self-schemas that emerge from social interaction with machines from an early age vary across individuals? How will people align themselves with or against the values of a machine-centered culture? The risks inherent in prognostication make it unwise to offer overly-definitive answers. However, in the present work, we seek to articulate some suggestions, predicated upon extrapolations from our current knowledge of IDs, and especially the emerging knowledge of their effects in human-machine interaction.

## 1.2. Anticipating the future: The cross-cultural analogy

In anticipating future shifts in paradigms for personality we are guided by cross-cultural research strategies. Like the past, the future is a foreign country. Despite sociotechnical change, we assume that dimensional structures for traits obtained 40 years from now will broadly but imperfectly resemble the Five Factor Model (FFM: McCrae, 2009), much like the real but imperfect alignment of Western with non-

Western personality structures (Church, 2016; Rollock & Lui, 2016). Thus, one approach to articulating a realistic future is to consider how the somewhat universal “etic” traits will govern an individual's response to interactions with intelligent machines. We review existing research on relationships between the major traits such as the FFM and measures of human-robot interaction. These case examples may serve to prefigure IDs in adapting to the challenges of future technology.

Cross-cultural perspectives also acknowledge culture-specific “emic” traits (Cheung, 2004). That is, in a society centered on advanced technology, there may be important ID factors that are absent, unexpressed or muted in smokestack, industrial societies. For comparison, consider Piedmont and Aycock's (2007) claim that qualities central to the FFM openness dimension emerged during such industrial epochs in response to the rising importance of IDs in creativity and reaction to novelty. We review the research on new ID measures covering these future-relevant constructs including attitudes to automation and autonomy, fear of robots, and the predisposition to anthropomorphize machines.

Both etic and emic traits promise to be important for IDs in communication with robots and intelligent software agents. A key technological advancement in this respect is the advent of social robots that can team with a human on the basis of a mutual understanding of the task at hand, their roles as team-members, and their mutual capacity for teamwork behaviors such as providing backup when needed (Ososky, Philips, Schuster & Jentsch, 2013). The machine's capacity to understand human communications, and to reply intelligently to its human partner are critical for successful teaming. We thus review the extant studies of IDs in communication functions to address these specific concerns. Beyond etic and emic traits, in 2060, there is a third, more radical possibility. Increasing human-machine symbiosis, accelerating rates of technological progress, and increased availability of data on the individual may create, or even force a shift in the unit of analysis for personality research. This transition may be from traits to an idiographic understanding based on massive individual-level data (or individual-machine system data). There is little in our existing literatures to directly inform this prospect, but we will offer some suggestions. The final topic we address is the practical implications of personality research for supporting and personalizing machine design. The machine's ability to “read” a human's personality can inform smart product design that tailors itself to the individual's needs and wants.

2. The five factor model and individual differences in humanmachine interaction

## 2.1. Theoretical orientation

We assume that FFM traits will remain predictive of core human outcomes such as influencing others (extraversion), vulnerability to stress and negative emotion (neuroticism) and advancing at work (conscientiousness) (see Matthews, Deary & Whiteman, 2009). The more interesting question is how these broad traits will moderate IDs in response to the novel challenges of future technologies, such as working with a humanoid robot, assigning important personal decisions to AI, and accepting a place in a society mediated by “big data” algorithms. Such challenges promise to be diverse, numerous, and difficult to anticipate.

The Cognitive Adaptive Theory of Traits (CATT: Matthews, 2008, 2018, 2020) defines traits as stable and coherent functional adaptations to environmental demands as well as opportunities that are mediated by multiple neural, cognitive and self-regulative processes. Traits are anchored (on a long chain) by their biological bases. Thus, they reflect the universal adaptive challenges faced by all humans. However, because major features of human socio-cultural environments are malleable, traits are not fixed biological attributes, but rather reflect the ways in which adaptive challenges are filtered and modulated by culture. For example, CATT links neuroticism to IDs in social threat management (Matthews, 2004). Threat from others is a universal challenge, but the predominant expressions of social threat and the normative strategies for coping with threat vary from culture to culture. It is expected that neuroticism-like dimensions will be found in all present and future cultures. However, neuroticism factors of 2060 will not precisely align with the contemporary dimension either psychometrically or conceptually, because threat sensitivity will reflect in part technologydriven threats such as losing one's job to a robot, social media ostracism, or having life choices controlled by AI systems.

Matthews et al. (2016) identified three broad categories of demand in relation to working with technology to which the individual must adapt. First, future technologies will be increasingly complex and as almost a necessary consequence, difficult for humans to comprehend. This will be especially true as big data and machine learning methods advance. Traits supporting capabilities for handling cognitive workload may here prove adaptive. To our present knowledge, these include extraversion (dual-tasking), emotional stability (working memory) and conscientiousness (task engagement) (see Matthews, 2008, for detailed review). A particular difficulty lies in our present inability to diagnose multiple sources of unexpected machine behavior. For example, an error made by an autonomous vehicle might reflect low-level sensor failure or a high-level misunderstanding of where the human wishes to go; vehicle behavior is thus difficult to understand. How humans adapt to, and cope with, such ascending levels of autonomous action will surely be a function of their profile of individuality.

At the highest level, epistemic rationality is under threat. In a world controlled by complex machines, it will be increasingly difficult to develop and maintain an accurate model of reality. Individuals high in neuroticism are sensitive to such uncertainty (Berenbaum, Bredemeier & Thompson, 2008), especially under stress (Boyes & French, 2010). So, this trait may be maladaptive for interaction with complex technologies. Conversely, openness may prove more beneficial to the individual in this context, especially given its links to intellectual engagement and scientific interests (Goff & Ackerman, 1992). However, openness is likely to be adaptive only to the extent that the human can develop a rational model for machine functioning. “Inscrutable” AI (Weld & Bansal, 2018), based on incomprehensible algorithms, may be especially frustrating for high openness individuals.

A second set of demands derives from interacting with machines with social agency (Matthews et al., 2016). Increasingly, machines and software agents simulate human functions that facilitate teaming, such as shared situation awareness, communication and expressed and actual behavioral support (Matthews, Panganiban, Lin, Long & Schwing, ; Panganiban, Matthews & Long, 2019). Wynne and Lyons (2018) identified features of autonomous systems that make them more likely to be perceived as team-mates. These include cognitive factors such as perceptions that the system has decision-making capabilities and can work with the human towards common goals. They also include socialemotional factors such as rich communication and expression of benevolence, warmth, and rapport with the human. Anthropomorphic features also promote perceptions of social agency (de Graaf & Ben Allouch, 2013). In fact, there is a large literature on how attributes of robots influence human evaluation of the machine, but it neglects the role of ID factors. Given evidence that people's interpersonal social behaviors transfer to their interactions with computers (Nass, Steuer & Tauber, 1994) and robots (Hamacher, Bianchi-Berthouze, Pipe & Eder, 2016), we may surmise that traits associated with social affiliation including extraversion and agreeableness will promote social perceptions and motivations towards intelligence machines.

The third category is the demands on self-regulation that follow from increasing machine authority over humans (Matthews et al., 2016). In some contexts, where machine capabilities outstrip those of humans, the latter may find themselves junior partners in the humanmachine team. For example, in a military intelligence context, an AI may be better than a human commander at deciding where humans should be deployed for information-gathering activities. Machines may also increasingly evaluate individual human performance and deliver potentially negative feedback, threatening both self-esteem and self-efficacy, as well as the quality of the relationship with the machine. Given their sensitivity to criticism (Servaas et al., 2013), those high in neuroticism may be especially vulnerable to the stress derived from being overseen by an artificial agent. One design solution that could mitigate these adverse effects would be to increase the transparency of the system (Lyons, 2013), providing the human with insight into what the machine is doing, as well as why and how it does it (if possible). Transparency would benefit people high in neuroticism because it would reduce uncertainty, and it would also be beneficial to those high in openness, as it would facilitate their intellectual engagement.

## 2.2. The FFM and information technology

There is a large literature on the FFM and the associated correlates of computer and internet use. These include studies of social media and of problematic or dysfunctional internet use (e.g., Hawi, Samaha & Griffiths, 2018; Stead & Bibby, 2017). This research is largely beyond our present scope, in that much of it does not directly concern the challenges associated with novel, intelligent technology. For example, social media platforms such as Facebook use advanced algorithms to harvest user data but their primary purpose for users is to facilitate conventional social interactions such as sharing personal stories. We focus here on IDs in interaction with automation, as well as emerging work on interactions with advanced robots and virtual agents, including communication with artificial systems.

Robert (2018) distinguished three areas for personality research on robots. First, there is the effect of human personality on human-robot interaction (HRI). Individuals more comfortable interacting with robots may be better adapted to the challenges of future technological innovations. Individuals high in extraversion and emotional stability are more likely to anthropomorphize robots and feel psychologically close to them (Salem, Lakatos, Amirabdollahian & Dautenhahn, 2015), and thus feel comfortable with autonomous robots (Syrdal, Dautenhahn, Woods, Walters & Koay, 2006). However, these close feelings do not necessarily translate into higher levels of trust (Robert, 2018). Second, the simulated personality of the robot may influence HRI. Extraverted robots make more positive impressions on humans than introverted ones do, but the effect may vary with the robot's role (Robert, 2018). The FFM has found to be useful for characterizing robot personalities (Santamaria & Nathan-Roberts, 2017). Third, HRI may be facilitated by similarity in human and robot personality. Extraverts typically prefer extraverted robots, with the opposite for introverts (Robert, 2018), although people prefer dissimilarity in some contexts (Zhang, Esterwood, Yang & Robert, 2019).

## 2.3. Interactions with automated systems

Automation promises to improve the human condition and quality of life by freeing individuals from routine work and chores so they can then pursue more engaging and fulfilling activities. However, technology can also have a downside in repurposing people as passive monitors of system display rather than active, skilled agents (Parasuraman & Wickens, 2008). Optimization and calibration of trust are critical for effective use of automation: the human must match trust to the true capabilities of the system, avoiding both over- and undertrust (J. D. Lee & See, 2004). IDs in complacency about technology are associated with expressions of over-trust, such as failing to check for malfunctions in automated systems (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). An important issue is whether personality variations in trust in humans generalize to trust in machines (Hancock, Kessler, Kaplan, Brill & Szalma, 2019a). Person factors in trust in machines have been a relatively neglected aspect of research (Hancock, 2011) but some studies demonstrate a role for the FFM. In self-report data (see also Chien, Sycara, Liu and Kumru (2016), Hancock et al., 2019b) found that agreeableness was associated with higher trust in machines, consistent with its role in human-to-human trust. Conscientiousness also predicted human-robot trust. Another study (Merritt & Ilgen, 2008) identified extraversion as a correlate of interpersonal trust and confirmed this trait was also associated with the propensity to trust in machines.

Studies based on behavioral data, focusing on IDs in monitoring roles, provide a more complex and nuanced pattern of results. Consistent with Merritt and Ilgen's (2008) findings, Kidwell, Calhoun, Ruff and Parasuraman (2012) found that extraverts preferred to set a higher level of automation, in simulated operation of multiple unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs). Szalma and Taylor (2011) had participants monitor a simulated video-feed from an unmanned ground vehicle (UGV) for threats such as improvised explosive devices (IEDs). Automation highlighted possible threats, with varying degrees of reliability. Some of these findings suggest generalization of the known correlates of the FFM to the specific automation scenario. For example, high neuroticism individuals tended to express higher workload and stress, and to perform more poorly. Other results appeared to be more specific to automation; for example, conscientious participants reported higher performance workload following a transition to conditions of lower demand and no automation support, perhaps reflecting their performance motives. Lin et al. (2019) found effects of neuroticism and conscientiousness in a simulation of performing surveillance tasks with support from automation during multi-UAV operation. As in Szalma and Taylor (2011), neuroticism was associated with higher stress. However, this trait predicted lower performance accuracy only when task demands themselves were low. High neurotic individuals may compensate for high demands through increased effort (c.f., Eysenck & Calvo, 1992). Highly conscientious individuals showed less dependence on automation under high demands, which was a counterproductive strategy given that attention tended to be overloaded and the automation was quite reliable. Their motivations to take charge of the situation and cope through the exercise of personal responsibility may thus be maladaptive in some automated environments.

## 2.4. Communication and social interaction

Much of the work reviewed in the preceding sections addresses wellestablished issues in human-machine interaction, such as trust, usability, and anxiety, from the standpoint of interactions with advanced technology. However, robots will increasingly acquire the capability of functioning like human teammates, maintaining a representation of progress towards task goals, monitoring the status of the human, and acting to maintain team cohesion and shared situation awareness, in addition to immediate task-directed activities (Chen & Barnes, 2014).

For human-robot teams, IDs in communication become increasingly important, in both human-to-robot and robot-to-human directions (Lyons, 2013). Robots can use multiple modalities for communication, including natural language. This capability adds fluidity to the humanrobot interaction allowing for speed of information transfer, task collaboration and learning (Mavridis, 2015). The combination of dialog capability, affective expression via word choice, tone and facial expression and eye gaze provide data which allow the human partner to build upon and use a theory of mind of the robot, supporting teaming. As robotic partners (RPs) evolve, humans may vary in their willingness to communicate with the artificial system. Thus, individual differences across potential human partners requires consideration before design of a “one size fits all” RP. This section addresses research touching on these issues, including studies of demographic factors (age, gender and culture) that point the way towards future studies of the role of traits.

Personality traits may moderate the human's interpretation and management of signals from the robot, but current HRI research is limited in scope. Beňuš et al. (2018) investigated IDs in the adaptation to natural speech that occurs between communicators, called entrainment. Participants played an adventure style decision-making game and received advice from a robotic/avatar partner. Pitch, intensity and speech rate was either matched (entrained) or mismatched (disentrained) to the agent partner's speech. Findings revealed that trust was higher in females working with the disentrained partner and that individuals high in openness also reported higher trust in the disentrained partner. Another study looked at engagement with an embodied robot during an assembly task (Ivaldi et al., 2017). The iCub robot performed a simple assembly task with color paper rolls. Extraversion scores were positively correlated with verbal communication with the robot but not with gaze at the robot.

Social robotics provides insight into variation in preferences for interaction with artificial systems. One relevant process is self-disclosure, the act of revealing personal information, feelings, and thoughts about oneself to others (Jourard, 1964). Recently, self-disclosure has been examined in human-robot interaction contexts. Some of this work has focused on how robot “personality” influences self-disclosure. Human engagement with an RP is enhanced when a virtual agent discloses highly intimate information about itself (Kang & Gratch, 2011), and when the robot is supportively responsive to human disclosure (Birnbaum et al., 2016).

Other studies focus on human characteristics. Interacting with a virtual agent may promote self-disclosure, especially among socially anxious people (Kang & Gratch, 2011). Moreover, when the virtual agent disclosed highly intimate information about itself, individuals felt more engaged during the interaction (Kang & Gratch, 2011). Self-disclosure is especially relevant to healthcare. The lack of evaluative threat perceived in an RP may encourage patients to provide more information about their medical condition, compared to disclosure to a human practitioner. Desideri, Ottaviani, Malavasi, di Marzio and Bonifacci (2019) found that individuals with higher trait anxiety reported higher negative affect during a cognitive assessment interview by a human than those interacting with a robot. A different perspective comes from work on the uncanny valley, the tendency for near-human objects to produce feelings of creepiness and revulsion. People differ in their sensitivity to the uncanny valley, and those high in neuroticism and trait anxiety are more prone to negative reactions to androids presented in videos (MacDorman & Entezari, 2015).

Interaction with an RP may depend on its “personality”. Tay, Jung and Park (2014) observed participant reactions to robots differing in gender (male or female), occupational role (healthcare or security) and extraversion trait (introversion or extraversion). Extraversion in an RP was preferred across both occupational roles while gender preference was based on role. However, preference for extraversion may have been confounded by operationalizing introversion in the robot, which paralleled signs of poor functioning. The introverted robot was programmed to move slowly and talk slowly and only respond when spoken to as opposed to displaying true autonomy. This study exemplifies not only the types of observations being conducted in HRI but the difficulty of manipulating personality in an RP.

Manipulation of communication style is straightforward, and studies have shown group differences for social interaction in age and culture. Children appear to welcome robots easily and 6–7 year olds accept “disagreeable” personalities in a robot and are less aware of personality style differences when compared to 8–11 year olds (Martínez-Miranda, Pérez-Espinosa, Espinosa-Curiel, Avila-George & Rodríguez-Jacobo, 2018). Similarly, older adults appear less negatively impacted by a dominant virtual avatar in a collaborative online game (desert-survival-task) and report lower perceptions of control from the avatar than younger adults (Rosenthal-von der Pütten, Straßmann, Yaghoubzadeh, Kopp & Krämer, 2019). Biases may also depend on the competence of the user. In a study of use of an online shopping aid, higher competence in computer use interacted with social vs. task-oriented communication style to affect reports of trust and perceived interactivity (Chattaraman, Kwon, Gilbert & Ross, 2019). Those low in competence found a task-oriented communication style functionally superior, as seen in greater ratings of perceived ease of use, self-efficacy of using the site and lower cognitive load. Findings indicate that there is room for research in fitting communication styles to personality traits related to cognitive performance. Assuming that culture relates to performance by bridging language and behavioral expectations (Rau, Li & Li, 2009), communication style can be matched to one's cultural background. In an aided price judgement task, Chinese participants had higher ratings of acceptance for robot recommendations when robots spoke implicitly when compared to German participants, potentially due to the congruence with the speaking style of the participant (Rau et al., 2009). It seems that acceptance of preference for interaction stems from the expectations of the human partner. Therefore, research in communication must first define the type of interaction before making recommendations. Individuals carrying out true teaming may prefer an RP similar to themselves, while those relying on a system to perform a difficult task may prefer a less social-oriented style. Identifying the context may point to better personality predictors of communication preference.

## 2.5. Future directions: adapting to machine agency

The studies reviewed confirm the role of the FFM in interactions with automation and robots, but specific relationships between traits and outcomes vary from study to study, likely reflecting moderator effects of a range of task and contextual factors (Szalma & Taylor, 2011). An important general theme is the impact of technology on adaptation to increasing machine agency in both task performance and social activities. The growing capacity of machines and software agents to make high-stakes decisions, to over-ride human judgment and even to meet social needs such as that for companionship raises multiple adaptive challenges whose resolution may be linked to personality factors. Indeed, especially for skilled performers and agents, the basic notion of giving up control to a machine may be unwelcome (Oron-Gilad, Szalma, Thropp & Hancock, 2005). Table 1 summarizes some specific challenges and how traits might relate to IDs in relevant outcomes such as trust, behavioral dependence on emotion, and affective outcomes. The roles of traits are somewhat speculative given current lack of evidence but the table suggests hypotheses for further investigation.

## 3. Beyond the Big Five: New constructs for human-technology interaction

In this section, we review work that introduces novel trait constructs beyond the FFM relevant to interactions between humans and technology. These traits may be indicative of the constructs that will assume increasing salience as human life is increasingly dominated by intelligent, autonomous systems, i.e., the “emic” traits of future culture. The simplest such constructs are those for positive and negative reactions to new technology, such as computer self-efficacy and anxiety. However, additional personality factors may be necessary to capture how people differ qualitatively in their mental models for advanced robots and other intelligent, autonomous agents.

## 3.1. Orientations towards computer technology

The technology acceptance model (TAM: Davis, 1985) aims to explain the determinants of use of computers and other information systems. Perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use are the primary factors influencing behavioral intentions, which in turn affect actual system use and attitudes to the technology (Davis, Bagozzi & Warshaw, 1989). Perceived usefulness refers to the individual's beliefs that using a particular system would enhance their job performance, and perceived ease of use refers to beliefs that using a particular system would be free of effort. Validation studies have attempted to measure the key constructs and confirm the relationships proposed by TAM (Lee, Kozar & Larsen, 2003). TAM scales are typically tailored to specific technologies of interest, and so vary from study to study. However, studies have generally confirmed the validity and reliability of measurement for TAM constructs for various technologies, situations, and tasks (Lee, Kozar & Larsen, 2003). A meta-analysis (King & He, 2006) found that perceived usefulness predicted behavioral intention more strongly than did perceived ease of use, although there was some heterogeneity across studies. Chau (1996) revealed that perceived ease of use may play a more crucial role in software acceptance, suggesting that the influence of the two constructs might well vary in different technology and system contexts.

As the most widely applied theoretical model in the information system domain, many studies have been performed by different researchers to investigate the impact of various external variables on acceptance. TAM dimensions are only modestly associated with standard personality traits. For example, Svendsen, Johnsen, Almås-Sørensen and Vittersø (2013) investigated attitudes towards a software tool in a sample of 1004 participants. Several associations between the FFM and TAM constructs were observed; e.g., extraversion was associated with higher perceived usefulness, ease of use and behavioral intention. However, the largest FFM – TAM correlation was 0.21, and none of the correlations with behavioral intention, the proximal influence on behavior, exceeded 0.15. Studies of other constructs suggest that IDs in computer self-efficacy predict technology acceptance in multiple contexts (Strudwick, 2015; Venkatesh & Davis, 1996).

Another important construct is computer anxiety, defined as the apprehension or fear derived from the need to use computer-based systems (Simonson, Maurer, Montag-Torardi & Whitaker, 1987). Its facets including anxiety about using the technology, specific negative cognitions about interactions, and broader attitudes towards computers and their societal impact (Weil, Rosen & Wugalter, 1990). Computer anxiety is, typically, modestly negatively associated with competence in using computers (Zeidner & Matthews, 2005). It is also appropriately related to technology acceptance constructs. Computer anxiety mediates the effect of system experience on perceived ease of use (Hackbarth, Grover & Yi, 2003), as well as mediating effects of experience and self-efficacy on attitude towards a network system (Cazan, Cocoradă & Maican, 2016). A meta-analysis of these effects (Maricutoiu, 2014) confirmed the moderate and negative associations

Some of the correlates of computer anxiety may be context-sensitive; for example, Strudwick (2015) found no evidence that it was associated with technology acceptance in nurses who were required to use a computer-based hospital information system. However, computer anxiety overlaps with anxiety about robots, although the latter may also evoke distinctive attitudes and emotions (de Graaf, Ben Allouch & Lutfi, 2016; Nomura, Kanda, Suzuki & Kato, 2008). Lotz, Himmel and Ziefle (2019) investigated factors influencing acceptance of collaborative robot team-mates in industrial settings. Major concerns for employees included being injured by the robot, losing one's job, and anxiety about robots. Quantitative data confirmed the applicability of TAM to behavioral intentions to work with robots. Computer anxiety was negatively associated with perceived usefulness and perceived ease of use, both of which correlated positively with behavioral intention. Lotz et al. (2019) results also identified additional factors feeding into acceptance, including enjoyment, computer playfulness and social norms.

## 3.2. Individual differences in mental models of the system

Previously, we identified trust as a key construct for individual differences in human-machine interaction (J. D. Lee & See, 2004; Schaefer, Chen, Szalma & Hancock, 2016). Future, autonomous systems will make intelligent decisions using algorithms based on techniques including machine learning and big data analyses that are difficult to communicate clearly to the human. As we have seen, trust in contemporary technologies can be linked to both the FFM (Merritt & Ilgen, 2008) and to more specialized traits such as computer self-efficacy and internet anxiety (Thatcher, Loughry, Lim & McKnight, 2007). However, given the transformative nature of advances in machine intelligence and autonomy, these constructs may not fully capture IDs in cognitive, affective and behavioral response to future technologies.

Several researchers have developed scales intended to assess attitudes and feelings about intelligent machines. Merritt, Unnerstall, Lee and Huber (2015) perfect automation schema (PAS) measure addresses people's expectations that advanced machines should be nearperfect. Studies of trust in automated decision aids have shown that PAS scores predict higher trust (Lyons & Guznov, 2019). The PAS consists of two subscales which are named as high expectations and allor-none thinking respectively. Associations between trust and subscale scores show some variation across studies (Lyons & Guznov, 2019). As expected, Merritt et al. (2015) found that the all-or-none thinking factor was predictive of decreased trust after the automation made errors. Other relevant measures include Lyons and Guznov's (2019) Human Interaction and Trust (HIT) scale which focuses on individuals’ intentions to rely on a robot. Schaefer's (2016) Trust Perception Scale – HRI, which has been validated as a situational measure of trust in a robot, is used to measure changes in trust as a state as human-robot interaction develops. Validation work on these measures is still at an early stage but they seem likely to extend the ID measures available to researchers.

A conceptual model for trust in intelligent systems developed by Matthews, Lin, Panganiban and Long (2019) discriminated conventional and novel trust antecedents (see Fig. 1). Conventional antecedents include various situational and personal factors identified in studies of existing automated technologies (see Hancock et al., 2011, for a review). Interacting with intelligent and autonomous systems introduces novel factors associated with reactions to the “inscrutability” of advanced AI and to the capacity of the system to function as a social agent. In human-robot teaming (HRT), operators may perceive the highly automated machine as either an advanced tool or a human-like teammate (Matthews et al. 2019). The mental model which is activated depends partly on external factors such as the robot having a humanlike appearance and functionality (Wynne & Lyons, 2018). However, there may also be individual biases towards one mental model or the other.

![](data:image/jpeg;base64,)

Fig. 1. Outline of the Matthews et al. (2019) trust model for interaction with an intelligent, autonomous robot.

Matthews et al. (2019) developed a new Robot Threat Assessment (RoTA) scale to differentiate these mental models. This scale required participants to rate trust in robots performing threat analyses using various methods in a series of security scenarios. Two distinct correlated dimensions were identified, interpreted as trust in robots as advanced tools and as humanlike teammates. Items defining the first factor referred to scenarios requiring the robot to function like a conventional machine in performing physics-based analyses for threat (e.g., detecting radiation). Items for the second factor referred to psychological judgments (e.g., detecting angry facial emotion) typically seen as the preserve of humans. A follow-up study (see Matthews et al. 2019) showed that the RoTA predicted trust in a robot performing threatdetection tasks using psychological cues in a 3-D simulation of an urban environment. These studies (Matthews et al. 2019) also showed some convergences and divergences of the RoTA with the PAS, NARS and HIT.

Dispositional tendencies to anthropomorphize systems, especially robots, may also influence IDs in the mental model. Waytz, Cacioppo and Epley (2010) defined anthropomorphism as a particular form of mental state attribution, which refers to the tendency of attributing humanlike characteristics to nonhuman agents. Their Individual Differences in Anthropomorphism Questionnaire (IDAQ) measures stable IDs in anthropomorphism toward nonhuman animals, natural entities, and technological devices. Individuals with greater anthropomorphic tendencies were more likely to trust a robot in making important decisions such as medical condition prediction, lie detection, and personnel selection (Waytz et al., 2010). Anthropomorphism is significantly related to personality (e.g. openness, neuroticism, and conscientiousness), age, relationship status, and personal connection to animals (Letheren, Kuhn, Lings & Pope, 2016). However, as with other novel traits, correlations with the FFM are small in magnitude (rs<0.2). Future work may further discriminate the various mental models that shape trust in intelligent, autonomous systems, and the ID dimensions linked to the model characteristics.

## 4. A unit of analysis revolution?

To this point, we have reviewed studies based on the conventional understanding of traits as stable, nomothetic ID factors, whether universal or specific to technological cultures. However, we have neglected to explore the almost necessary conceptual dissonance that confronts those who study personality. This is because researchers’ interests are almost inevitably suspended between the exigencies of the normative and specificities of the idiographic. It is across this latter part of this overall research domain that true individual differences feature. Some facets of individual differences represent an enterprise that looks to reduce seven and one half billion human individuals into only a small number of discrete and formal categories. It is rather natural for behavioral scientists to search $\mathbf { f o r } ,$ and identify, the grouped dimensions of human behavior that remain consistent and predictable. After all, nomothetic and prospective theories and models rely upon the future being essentially similar $\mathbf { t o } ,$ and consistent with, the past. Imagine, if only for a moment, the counterfactual case where all was in flux. Constancy and prediction would be completely negated and William James’ “blooming, buzzing confusion” (James, Burkhardt, Bowers & Skrupskelis, 1890) would hold sway. In behavioral terms, the identification of largely stable personality traits allows us to say something useful, but not deterministic, about future behaviors. But now, into the expanding fluidity of the modern context of human behavior, fostered and fueled by technological expansion, these general designations are coming under challenge. We are being forced into a re-casting of what we understand by state and trait identifications. Here we consider, albeit briefly, the ramifications of these contemporary evolutions in both the content and context of performance.

The most important social force which provides the essential impetus for this re-evaluation of traditional approaches is technology. Here, we consider a brief, but polemic, gedanken experiment. Let us envision that we were able to describe, in exhaustive detail, each and every living individual's psychological state and prospective propensities. In such circumstances, would we have any necessity for groupbased or nomothetic characterizations? It is certain that in the past we have been able to use these group designations in order to reduce uncertainty about future behavior. Hence, personality assessments have played important, valuable, and effective roles in fields such as training and selection. This has been evident, especially as institutions have sought to better identify the most appropriate (fittest) personnel for particular tasks or pursuits. Yet modern computational power is not so limited as it once was. Seven billion floating point operations (flops) is not nearly so prohibitive as it would sound to the computer scientists of forty years ago. Thus, digital descriptions of each and every living human is not only feasible, but is the active goal of many commercial, as well as governmental enterprises today. In such circumstances, knowing how a certain individual ‘scores’ on a particular standardized test promises to add little to the veracity of their ‘shadow’ avatar that already represents a virtual emulation of them in a fully interactive computational space. Thus, we believe it will not be the degree of divergence of each individual from a nomothetic ‘prototype’ that will be of future concern. Rather, it is this individual ‘individuated’ and bespoken profile which will be the featured unit of personality analysis (Hancock, Hancock & Warm, 2009). Make no mistake, we still see practical emphases in commercial organizations in creating, validating, and using amenable collective descriptions for their immediate exploitation. However, the future is individual not collective - and this is not all.

We anticipate that there will be another seismic shift in focus which we refer to as the “unit of analysis” revolution. Here, we can ask a simple, if frightening, question. Can we part people from their smartphones? Today, this separation is sometimes taken as almost a comedic inquiry. However, contemporary research shows that, even when expressed as a threat rather than an actuality, the prospect of smartphone loss can cause excessive stress. Indeed, a four-factor scale for nomophobia, the fear of being out of mobile phone contact, has recently been published (Yildirim & Correia, 2015). In large part, these fears arise because these mobile hand-held computers are no longer an adjunct to life but a conduit to it. If Jean Anthelme Brillat-Savarin was correct when he asserted ‘you are what you eat,” it may now be equally legitimate to now assert “you are what you access.” Our point is a simple one. The forthcoming “unit of analysis” will not be the dissociated individual human, but will be that individual in-tandem with the electronic umbilical connection that links them to the wider world.

Here, we must then ask whether technology (in all its forms such as robots, automated vehicles, etc.) is actually becoming part of an individual's personality? It is easy initially to dismiss such a proposition since our discipline of psychology has traditionally always featured the primacy of the single, dissociated individual as the central focus of attention. But the world is changing. The boundary specifications of this emerging unit of analysis are manifestly evolving. Therefore, the specific question is whether the now (almost) obligatory technical appendage represents a modifier $\mathbf { t o } ,$ or even extension of, each individual's personality profile? We understand that this question can seem at least strange, if not even bizarre. Of course, technology does not necessarily mutilate the natural profile of someone's personality. The technology may become an expression of personality; another, if more complex, manifestation of the ‘behavioral residue’ of personality (Gosling, Ko, Mannarelli & Morris, 2002). Yet, no one studying experimental psychology, or especially human-machine interaction research, would balk at the statement that modern technology tends to induce substantive changes in cognition (Sparrow, Liu & Wegner, 2011). We anticipate that in the next forty years, the ubiquity and reach of technology will profoundly influence personality and individual differences also.

## 5. Personality and the design of technology

Following on from previous sections, we can now transition to the applied question of how IDs research can inform the design of advanced technologies to operate as effective collaborative partners, adapting to our needs and capabilities, given the increasing symbiosis of human and artificial systems (Gill, 2012; Hancock, 2007). Traditional design principles have emphasized the features of the technology that impact perception, cognition, and physiological response. However, there is growing recognition that not only do we shape technology to support information processing, but our technological environment reciprocally shapes our own perceptions and cognitions (Hancock, 2009). In a similar manner, the technological landscape is shaped by our affective traits and states, and the technological ecosystem can in turn influence those states and the expression of traits (Szalma, 2009, 2014).

Szalma (2009) established an initial framework of principles and guidelines for incorporating such IDs into research and design for human-technology interaction. A crucial step in the design of any system and its interfaces is a detailed analysis of the tasks humans will use the technology to complete $( \mathbf { i } . \mathbf { e } . ,$ task analysis). Szalma (2009) argued that in order to include personality (and IDs in general) in the design process, there should be an analogous ‘person analysis’. However, the theoretical framework and core personality constructs for such an analysis remain to be specified. The community of personality researchers has a substantial and important contribution to make to this endeavor. Research in human-technology interaction, and practitioners who design those interfaces, will be compelled to incorporate IDs in their future designs, in part because of the trend we have noted toward individuation in design (Hancock et al., 2009). Without the contribution of personality researchers, the application of affective states and traits to technology design will likely remain fragmented, incomplete, and limited in its effectiveness. We examine next how personality and individual difference considerations in the design of technology may progress from static, to customized, and finally to adaptive technologies.

Products, and their components, offer different types of user accommodation: choice, customization, and adaptation. Conventional “static” products offer little or no flexibility to accommodate variation in personality and individual differences once designed. The needs or preferences of different users can be accommodated by offering a choice of different products or product configurations. In this case, the challenge for designers becomes one of accommodating each of the various

IDs of a target user base. The challenge for consumers is then finding the appropriate product type or configuration to best fit their own particular needs. Consumers currently depend very heavily on other consumer's reviews to inform their personal design selection. However, this source of information is often biased (e.g., Li & Hitt, 2008). Further, as future technology becomes more complex and fulfillment of projected needs is more difficult (especially when individual users lack prior experience with similar products), users may find it exceedingly difficult to make the appropriate technology selection decisions without further assistance. A tool designed to assist consumers with technology selection, whether web-based or as a tool for salespeople, may provide useful assistance, but such a tool would require a well-grounded, systematic understanding of consumer needs and how each technology fits those needs.

In the same way that design and choice of static products should be informed by personality and individual differences insights, technology customization must also be so informed. Beyond providing traditional affordances for individual preferences (e.g., usability choices and esthetic – hedonic – flexibility), customization should provide choice in how a task is approached and executed. It must also meet the abilities of the user and encourage skill improvement (e.g., role settings), and, mindful of the social implications of use of the technology, should allow customization for relatedness (e.g., privacy settings; Szalma, 2014). In the case of customization, several factors influence the design solution. To identify them, task analysis for customization should 1) identify relevant user subgroups, 2) observe group differences in the context of task and tool use, 3) estimate each group's different requirements and derive design implications (Lottridge, Chignell & Straus, 2011). A similar analysis could also support customization at the level of the individual. Each task analysis step would benefit from a strong pre-existing empirical understanding of ID factors, particularly as future technology allows for exponentially more customization and vetting of all possible bespoken options and configurations is not possible.

Design implementation will additionally require mapping customization options onto user expectations, which will also become more difficult and nuanced with technology complexity. Users may become overwhelmed by the sheer number of options afforded to them and may require guidance to identify coherent option combinations. Some car designs, for example, allow for several driving parameters to be adjusted (e.g., steering sensitivity, transmission tuning, suspension tuning, efficiency options, engine power), but provide presets to fit general goals (comfort, economy, sport, super-sport). These options, their combinations, and how they are communicated to the user/customer (e.g., what does a “sport” setting mean to different users?) can all be informed by a strong understanding of personality and individual differences research. The future research we have outlined is necessary to augment existing knowledge.

Dynamic products, especially those like Siri that utilize anthropomorphic features (Luger & Sellen, 2016), present even greater challenges than do static and one-time customizable products. They also provide unique opportunities. To be adaptive, dynamic products require sources of data, and a well-designed product must be based on a strong understanding of the meaning of that source data and the appropriate response to what that data indicates about the person using it. In other, words technology should be “user literate” (Browne, 1990). For these products, an understanding of personality and individual differences proves critical. For more advanced technologies that serve more as teammates than tools, research on human-human interaction and personality compatibility can serve as a strong starting point for implementing an appropriate design solution and conventions for adapting to different user types (Sarsam & Al-Samarraie, 2018). Using a pre-existing, theory-based understanding of IDs and some initial information about each user (e.g., personality survey on setup), technology can be calibrated appropriately for individual user needs from the very first interaction.

Since the application of basic theoretical research to each given context is not likely to be straightforward, the design of adaptive products may require long lead times during which different implementation and adaption strategies are vetted. Fortunately, finetuning of design solutions can be continued after such products are fielded. To function, adaptive products must continuously gather data to infer user state and context. Instead of flushing this data, it can be stored and used to calibrate pattern recognition conventions for specific individuals, or their personal avatars as previously discussed. User data could be generated based on direct interaction with the human (e.g., statements, requests, behavioral responses, etc.) or gathered from physiological recordings (e.g., Starr, 2013; Wohleber, 2016) as and when context allows (Wohleber, Matthews, Funke & Lin, 2016). Additionally, there are other sources that provide ongoing insight into a user's personality, including the physical spaces that they inhabit (Gosling et al., 2002), their social media profiles (Back et al., 2010), and their interactions with other humans (Letzring, 2008). In addition to informing adaptation for the product itself based on individual users (identifying long-term trends and successful and unsuccessful adaptations to various user states), data can inform product-wide updates based on the accumulated observations of interactions with other products.

Smart products that gather data to inform technology adaptation already exist (e.g., Mortensen, 2019). However, the extent to which scientific theory informs, and is informed by, adaptive product implementations is not clear. Atheoretical, big data approaches might prove pragmatically useful, but a strong scientific understanding of IDs is critical to inform new approaches, new designs, and new implementations of known adaptive technologies (Kao & Venkatachalam, 2018). Such inter-connectivity will help to build a sophisticated and reliable knowledge-base. To augment a scientifically informed knowledge-base of human-technology interaction, data collected for each user could also be used to test theory on a continuous basis. Thus, various approaches to working with different personality types can be dynamically evaluated (as different instructional approaches are tested in the classroom). Products can be updatable and updated to allow for new theories and methods to utilize existing user data. Each update might recalibrate how the product understands its user. Further, as technology advances to become more and more like a separate culture, in comparison with the present day, new emic traits (Cheung, 2004) might be discovered which characterize IDs in these more technology immersed societies of the future.

A critical consideration, as technology moves toward online data gathering, user research-driven products, is the protection of user privacy (Horvitz & Mulligan, 2015). Use of technology that records and analyses user data has potentially problematic ramifications. For example, a system utilizing AI could discover personality disorders of which the individual may or may not be aware. A benign AI might use this information therapeutically. Alternatively, dissemination of such information (legally or illicitly) could undermine the person's wellbeing and sense of worth, as well as their reputation in the electronic ecosphere. The human and artificial gatekeepers of the AI's data stores could acquire substantial power over the individual. Thus, product design should incorporate appropriate etiquette (Hancock, 2011). This form of machine politeness includes keeping sensitive personal information confidential. With technology that evidently interacts more as other humans might, keeping sensitive information confidential presents a bigger challenge than might first be apparent. Communication protocols may be required which disguise the nature of interactions to preserve privacy when under observation (e.g., sensitive topics and even methods of interaction may need to be reserved only for secure contexts to avoid third party interference). Strong and transparent privacy protection policies would encourage use of these advanced technologies, allowing for a more complete profile of potential users. The lack of effective privacy conventions would result in fractures of trust (Schaefer et al., 2016), which then constrain knowledge-bases, since a portion of the population would opt out to maintain privacy (and this portion would likely differ systematically in personality relative to the technology-accepting population). From an IDs perspective, future research may identify those factors that regulate willingness to routinely broadcast personal data into cyberspace, as opposed to taking the sometimes arduous steps that are necessary to limit the data flow.

## 6. Conclusion

Personality research must necessarily evolve to keep pace with sociotechnological change and the novel adaptive challenges posed by the AI and social agency of advanced machines. Here, we have advocated for the continuing relevance of current trait models, but we have highlighted the need to investigate traits which are more closely tied to the adaptive challenges of interaction and cooperation with intelligent autonomous systems. We also anticipate a return of idiographic perspectives fueled by big data on each and every individual. These various evolutionary and revolutionary perspectives may contribute to the applied benefits of future personality research, especially self-adaptive technology that optimizes the symbiotic relationship. We conclude here with three foci for future research.

## 6.1. Personality assessment

Capturing the essentials of personality in dimensional models will remain a central preoccupation for researchers. We anticipate a relatively slow evolution of the FFM and cognate broad-trait models in response to the changing demands and opportunities of the sociotechnical environment, consistent with projections from CATT (Matthews, 2018). It will be increasingly important to supplement general trait models with novel dimensions which capture key features of the person-technology interaction. Whether new superfactors emerge, such as a broad technophilia/technophobia dimension, remains to be seen. The idiographic perspective hints at a more radical departure from such standard assessment methodologies.

## 6.2. Processes and outcomes

Currently, neuroscience, cognitive and social psychology provide theories that define processes mediating between traits and outcomes. Cognitive and social processes will require redefinition to cover the expertise necessary to navigate the future world. Neuroscience perspectives may have more durability, though we note the need to incorporate stronger psychophysiological metrics for human-technology interaction. Further into the future, the advent of cyborgs in which brain function is artificially augmented looms on the horizon. The outcomes addressed by process models will also evolve. For example, we have registered the importance of trust and automation-dependence emerging from current research. Perhaps the greatest challenge will be to balance the intense focus on the individual human-machine system, as suggested by the idiographic approach, with the vision of the person as embedded in complex human-machine networks facilitated by the internet.

## 6.3. Applications

Personality research supports a wide range of applications in clinical, occupational, educational, and other contexts (Matthews et al., 2009). Developments in assessment and in explanatory, process-based models will enhance traditional applications of personality assessment in domains such as personnel selection and clinical diagnosis. For example, measures of trust in technology may be important for selecting information technology workers and for diagnosing and treating conditions such as nomophobia. Beyond these evolutionary advances, there is also scope for more revolutionary applications. We have highlighted how consumer psychology is advancing from customization of products to intelligent, self-personalizing product design. More generally, applied benefits may be provided by robots or virtual agents that function as socially-competent teammates, capable of understanding the person as an individual, communicating through natural language, and learning from experience. We may look forward to a future of artificial therapists, teachers, life coaches, chauffeurs, personal assistants, and even companions, all tailored to the needs, competencies and vulnerabilities of the individual.
